The Barber surgeonfish *Acanthurus bahianus*, a common herbivore on Caribbean and Atlantic reefs, exhibits life-history traits that are broadly consistent with those of other acanthurids. Field studies indicate that individuals typically attain a total length of approximately 17 cm [Li = approximately 17 cm] at the end of their growth trajectory. This asymptotic size is associated with a corresponding ultimate wet body mass of about 76.4 grams [Wwi = about 76.4 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions collected across multiple reef sites. The onset of sexual maturation, defined here as the total length at which 50% of individuals possess mature gonads, occurs at a considerably smaller body size. Survey data from the genus suggest that puberty is reached at a total length of 8 cm [Lp = 8 cm], at which point the average individual has a wet body mass of approximately 8.4 grams [Wwp = approximately 8.4 grams]. This size-based threshold for reproductive readiness is notably lower than that of some larger-bodied surgeonfishes, likely reflecting a strategy that prioritizes early reproductive output in an environment with relatively high adult mortality.

Reproductive output in *A. bahianus* can be described through the gonadosomatic index (GSI), which expresses gonad mass as a proportion of total body mass. At a stable temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the gonadosomatic index was recorded at 9% [GSI = 9%]. This value, originally documented in the congener *Acanthurus nigrofuscus*, suggests a moderate reproductive investment relative to body size, a pattern consistent with the iteroparous, batch-spawning strategy typical of the genus. The reproductive output per spawning event is directly influenced by this somatic-to-gonadal tissue ratio, with gravid females capable of producing hundreds of pelagic eggs during a single spawning bout.

Early life stages of *A. bahianus* are characterized by a very small initial mass, a consequence of the diminutive egg size typical of pelagic-spawning teleosts. Based on an egg diameter of 0.7 mm, a measurement reported for the closely related *Acanthurus lineatus*, the wet weight at birth for a newly hatched yolk-sac larva of this surgeonfish is estimated at 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams]. This minute lecithotrophic larva represents the starting point for a rapid growth trajectory that will eventually lead to the 76.4 gram [Wwi = 76.4 gram] adult mass observed in asymptotic individuals. The transition from the endotrophic, yolk-dependent stage to exogenous feeding occurs within a few days post-hatching, a critical period during which larval survival is heavily dependent on the availability of suitable planktonic prey. The vast difference between the hatchling mass and the mass at puberty of 8.4 grams [Wwp = 8.4 grams] underscores the substantial energetic demands of the pelagic larval and juvenile phases that precede settlement onto the reef.

The duration of the entire post-settlement life cycle is finite and strongly influenced by ambient temperature. For a surgeonfish residing in waters at a stable 28 °C [T = 28 °C], the maximum documented lifespan, or longevity, is approximately 32 years [am = approximately 32 years]. This substantial lifespan, which equates to roughly 11,680 days [am = roughly 11,680 days] under these same thermal conditions, p at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C]laces *A. bahianus* among the longer-lived members of its family, a trait that is likely linked to its gradual growth trajectory and relatively late attainment of ultimate size. Individuals that achieve the species' ultimate total length of 17 cm [Li = 17 cm] have therefore invested many years in somatic growth before reaching terminal body size. The 32-year longevity estimate (32 years) [am = 32 years] is particularly notable given the small to moderate adult body mass of this species, which typically correlates with shorter lifespans in many other teleost lineages at a temperature of 28 °C [T = 28 °C].

Comparative analyses across surgeonfishes reveal that the 8 cm [Lp = 8 cm] total length at puberty observed in *A. bahianus* is associated with a wet body mass at that developmental milestone of 8.4 grams [Wwp = 8.4 grams]. This puberty point occurs well before the species attains its maximum size of 17 cm [Li = 17 cm], ensuring a prolonged window of reproductive activity spanning many years. The substantial growth increment between the 8.4 gram [Wwp = 8.4 gram] mass at sexual maturity and the adult ultimate wet weight of 76.4 grams [Wwi = 76.4 grams] indicates that significant somatic investment continues well after the onset of reproductive capability. This pattern of early maturation followed by continued growth is common among iteroparous reef fishes that face size-dependent predation and competition. In summary, the life history of *A. bahianus* is quantitatively defined by a small hatchling mass of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams], a gonadosomatic index of 9% [GSI = 9%] at 28 °C [T = 28 °C], and a maximum longevity of 32 years [am = 32 years].
